quote: Imported modules keep their bytecode in a cache until their source changes
problem: The book has never said what a Python module is or what importing one means. The word "import" appears nowhere earlier, and the only modules so far were kernel modules. So the reader cannot tell which of a program's code gets cached and which does not, yet the figure's lane title ("Python · an imported module") and the caption depend on that difference. Only the closed strip says that a script run directly is recompiled every time.
fix: a module is a code file another file loads with `import`; the file you run is recompiled each run
reason: 'import' and 'module' are never introduced in Parts I-II (only kernel modules). The p3 sentence and the Fig 7.1 lane title 'an imported module' both lean on a distinction the reader cannot parse. The closed strip only half answers it (a script run directly is recompiled).
judge_fix: p3: "Imported modules (code files that a program loads with `import`) keep their bytecode in a cache until their source changes; the interpretation is paid for on every run." Strip is already consistent with this.

quote: 3.13: optional build, no GIL
problem: The drawing never expands or explains GIL (only the hidden desc spells out 'global interpreter lock'), so this reader cannot say what the 2024 build took out or why it ends the timeline. It is explained later at ch7-gil, section 04 of this chapter.
fix: expand it and point ahead in a few words, e.g. 'no GIL (the one-thread-at-a-time lock of §04)'
reason: Fig 7.2's last label uses 'GIL' two sections before it is defined (section 04). The book's own rule is to name a term before using it, and the caption does not mention the GIL, so a reader who studies the timeline meets an unexplained acronym.
judge_fix: Label: "3.13: optional build, no GIL (Section 04)". If that does not fit at 375 px with labels of at least 11 px, put the pointer in the caption instead: "...retired in 2020; in 2024 Python 3.13 first offered a build without the lock of Section 04." (keeps two sentences).

quote: Text became Unicode
problem: Unicode has not been taught anywhere up to here (no earlier section and no KNOWN TERM), so this reader cannot say what Python 2's text was or why changing it broke old code.
fix: a short gloss, e.g. 'text became characters from any alphabet (Unicode), not raw bytes'
reason: Unicode appears nowhere in Parts I-II. The strip line states that text became Unicode and that this broke code, with no hint of what Python 2 text was.
judge_fix: Combine with finding 5 in the strip line: "*What 3.0 fixed.* Text became Unicode (characters from any alphabet, where Python 2 text was plain bytes), `1/2` became 0.5 (it was 0), and `print \"x\"` became `print(\"x\")`: each one broke old code."

quote: 1/2 became 0.5, and print became a function: each one broke old code
problem: The old behaviour is never given (1/2 used to give 0 because whole-number division dropped the remainder; print was a statement written without brackets), so this reader cannot see what changed or why old code broke.
fix: put the old form beside each: '1/2 (was 0)', 'print "x" became print("x")'
reason: The strip says 1/2 'became 0.5' and print 'became a function' without the old behaviour. The reader cannot see what changed or why old code broke. Facts check out: Python 2 gave 1/2 == 0 (whole-number division) and print was a statement written without brackets.
judge_fix: Same line as finding 4: `1/2` became 0.5 (it was 0), and `print "x"` became `print("x")`.

id: ch7-types-p4 (Fig 7.3 How it works, 'The middle way')
quote: Type hints with typing.Protocol let a checker such as mypy verify the contract
problem: The section has just said Python variables carry no declared types, so this reader cannot tell what a 'type hint' is, where it is written, what a Protocol states, or how a checker can know types before the program runs; nothing earlier in the book defines any of these.
fix: say that type hints are optional type labels the programmer writes, which the interpreter ignores and a separate checker reads; a Protocol lists the methods an object must have
reason: 'Type hints', 'typing.Protocol' and 'mypy' occur only in this strip line. The section's prose says Python variables carry no declared types, so the reader has nothing to attach the terms to. Expert jargon used once with no gloss breaks law 4.
judge_fix: "*The middle way.* Type hints are optional type labels you write in the code. Python ignores them when the program runs, but a checker such as mypy reads them first; a `typing.Protocol` lists the methods an object must have, so the contract \"must have `speak()`\" is checked beforehand, without any shared parent class."

quote: or running C code, can let go of the lock
problem: Two sections back (ch7-interpret-p3) the reader learned that CPython is a C loop that runs C code for every opcode, so every Python thread is already running C code. They cannot tell which C code this means (a C library the program calls) or why that code may drop the lock when the interpreter's own C code may not.
fix: name it as a C library the program calls, which works on its own data and touches no Python object's count
reason: Section 01 just taught that CPython is a C loop running C code for every opcode, so 'running C code' now reads as true of every Python thread. The clause means a C library the program calls that works on its own data (as NumPy does in section 06). Wording is ambiguous in context.
judge_fix: "...though a thread waiting on the network, or calling a C library that works on its own data, can let go of the lock."

quote: For thousands of network waits, Python's `asyncio` shares one thread among many tasks
problem: p1 has just said that a thread waiting on the network lets go of the lock, so threads already handle waits, and the reader cannot say what asyncio gains over one thread per wait. The p4 caption's 'no locks' benefit does not settle it, because p2 told them the GIL already runs one thread at a time.
fix: one clause: each thread costs memory and kernel switches and can be switched at any point; tasks are cheap and switch only at await
reason: p1 has just said a thread waiting on the network releases the lock, so the reader fairly asks why asyncio is needed. The p4 caption's 'no locks' benefit does not answer the cost question. The reason (a thread per wait costs memory and kernel switches) is standard and takes one clause.
judge_fix: "For thousands of network waits, where a thread apiece would cost too much memory and too many switches, Python's `asyncio` shares one thread among many tasks, each handing it over only where it says `await`, as the Bridge's cooperative programs yielded (Fig 7.5)."

quote: PEP 703's free-threaded build uses per-object locks and biased reference counting
problem: This is in Fig 7.4's How it works strip. The prose said that a lock on every object slowed code by 30–50%, and now the cheap new design is said to use per-object locks too. 'Biased reference counting', the only thing offered as the difference, is never explained, so a reader who opens the strip ends up more confused than before.
fix: a plain clause: the thread that owns an object updates its count without a lock, and only other threads pay for one
reason: The prose blames 'a lock on every object' for the 30-50% slowdown; the strip then credits the cheap design with 'per-object locks', which reads as the same thing, and 'biased reference counting' is unexplained. Checked against PEP 703 (peps.python.org/pep-0703): per-object locks guard only containers (list, dict, set); biased reference counting lets the owning thread update its count with plain non-atomic operations while other threads use slower atomic ones. The finding's suggested fix ('only other threads pay for a lock') is slightly wrong, since it is atomic operations, not a lock.
judge_fix: "*Removing it.* PEP 703's free-threaded build gives each object an owner: the owning thread updates its reference count with cheap plain operations, other threads with slower atomic ones, and per-object locks guard only lists, dicts and sets. In 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs somewhat slower in it." (Source: PEP 703, 'Biased Reference Counting' and 'Container Thread-Safety'.)

quote: read the digits out of both
problem: From Chapter 2 the reader thinks of an int as a fixed-width binary number. Nothing says what 'digits' an int object holds or why they have to be read out, so step 5 cannot be explained back. (CPython stores an int as a row of base-2^30 'digits' so it can grow without limit, and the book never says so.)
fix: 'read the numbers out of both', or one strip line: a Python int has no size limit, so its value is stored as a row of chunks
reason: Minor. 'Digits' reads as decimal digits or as a fixed-width binary number from Chapter 2; CPython actually stores an int as a row of base-2^30 chunks. A one-word change removes the false picture; the step needs no more than that.
judge_fix: Step 5: "read the values out of both".

quote: the interpreter specialises hot instructions once it has seen their types
problem: Neither 'hot' (run often) nor 'specialises' (swaps in a faster instruction for the types it has seen) has been defined. Specialising is explained later in the fig-7-7 strip. 'Hot' is never explained; the ch7-interpret strip also used it without a definition.
fix: 'once an instruction has run often, the interpreter swaps in a faster version for the types it keeps seeing'
reason: 'Hot' is first used undefined in the ch7-interpret strip and again here; 'specialises' is only explained in the next figure's strip, which comes after this one. Both are cheap to gloss at first use.
judge_fix: Fig 7.6 strip: "...and the interpreter swaps a faster, specialised instruction in for one that keeps meeting the same types, such as `BINARY_OP_ADD_INT`." And at first use in the ch7-interpret strip: "turn hot bytecode (the parts that run most often) into machine code while the program runs."

quote: using computed gotos where the compiler supports them
problem: 'Computed gotos' is never explained. 'The compiler' here means the C compiler that builds CPython, but this section has just used 'the compiler' for CPython's bytecode stage (p2), so the reader cannot tell what supports what.
fix: drop the expert term, or 'jumps straight from one handler to the next where the C compiler that builds CPython allows it'
reason: 'Computed gotos' is expert detail the book never uses again, and 'the compiler' here means the C compiler that builds CPython while the same section has used 'the compiler' for CPython's bytecode stage. Nothing downstream needs it (law 4).
judge_fix: "*The loop.* `ceval.c` jumps straight from each instruction to its C handler."

quote: multiplying two 1000 × 1000 matrices (grids of numbers) takes a billion multiply-adds
problem: The section says a matrix is a 'grid of numbers' but never says what multiplying two of them involves. A reader who multiplies cell by cell gets a million operations, so they cannot see where a billion comes from. Fig 7.9's caption and its 'three nested loops' strip both lean on that billion.
fix: a clause: each of the million answer cells is one row times one column, 1000 products added up
reason: The billion is the number the whole section leans on (Fig 7.9 caption and strip), but the reader is only told what a matrix is, not how multiplying two gives 10^9; cell-by-cell thinking gives a million. The strip's 'three nested loops' comes later and only for readers who open it. One clause supplies it.
judge_fix: "...multiplying two 1000 × 1000 matrices (grids of numbers) takes a billion multiply-adds, because each of the million cells of the answer is 1000 products added up, and NumPy hands the job to BLAS, a decades-old library of hand-tuned routines (Fig 7.8)."

quote: works on _any_ object that has a `read()` method (a file, a network socket, a stand-in for testing)
problem: A Python socket has no read() method. socket.socket offers recv() and send(); on CPython 3.14, hasattr(socket.socket(), 'read') is False. Only sock.makefile() and ssl.SSLSocket have read(). The example meant to show duck typing working names an object that would actually raise AttributeError, which is the exact failure Fig 7.3 shows.
fix: "(a file, an HTTP response, a stand-in for testing)". http.client.HTTPResponse has read(). Checked locally on CPython 3.14.0: socket.socket has no read(); makefile() and SSLSocket do.
reason: Checked on CPython 3.14.0: hasattr(socket.socket(),'read') is False. A plain socket would raise AttributeError, the very failure Fig 7.3 shows. Real example in ch7-types-p3.
judge_fix: ch7-types-p3: "(a file, an HTTP response, a stand-in for testing)". http.client.HTTPResponse has read().

quote: Dynamically typed languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby) check types at runtime.
problem: The paragraph then says the same program "dies there with a `TypeError`". That is true for Python and Ruby but not for JavaScript, which usually converts the value and carries on: f("5") with n*2 returns 10, and f("abc") returns NaN, with no error. A reader comes away thinking JavaScript fails loudly the way Python does. JavaScript's silent coercion is the textbook counterexample, and Section 02 points at it when it calls Python's `1 + "a"` an error "rather than a guess".
fix: Simplest: "Dynamically typed languages (Python, Ruby) check types at runtime." Or keep JavaScript and scope the next sentence: "The same Python program starts without complaint, runs until it reaches the mistake, and dies there with a `TypeError`; JavaScript often converts the value instead and carries on."
reason: Checked with node: n*2 on "5" gives 10 and on "abc" gives NaN, with no error. The sentence "dies there with a TypeError" is false for JavaScript, which the same sentence lists.
judge_fix: ch7-types-p2: "Dynamically typed languages (Python, Ruby, Lisp) check types at runtime." Leave the next sentence as is. (Alternative that keeps JavaScript: "...dies there with a `TypeError`; JavaScript would often convert the value and carry on.")

quote: Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost nothing at run time
problem: This misstates Stroustrup's zero-overhead principle and contradicts Chapter 6. Ch6 (ch6-zerocost-p1) gives the principle as "you do not pay for what you do not use, and what you do use is as fast as anything you could have written by hand" and calls the slogan "slightly misleading". ch6-stroustrup-p5 says a virtual method costs a hidden pointer and an indirect call. Stroustrup never held that abstractions cost nothing, only that they cost no more than hand-written code.
fix: "Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost no more at run time than the code you would have written by hand". Source: Stroustrup, The Design and Evolution of C++ (1994): "What you don't use, you don't pay for. And further: What you do use, you couldn't hand code any better."
reason: "Must cost nothing at run time" contradicts ch6-zerocost-p1 ("as fast as anything you could have written by hand", slogan "slightly misleading") and ch6-stroustrup-p5 (a virtual method costs a hidden pointer and a call). Stroustrup's formulation is "what you do use, you couldn't hand code any better" (Design and Evolution of C++, 1994).
judge_fix: ch7-datasci-p5: "Stroustrup held that an abstraction must cost no more at run time than the code you would have written by hand; van Rossum held that its real cost was paid in human attention, and would spend a hundred machine cycles to save a programmer five minutes."

quote: Every Python statement becomes hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop, plus the actual work.
problem: This overstates simple statements by about two times on today's CPython, and "Every" makes it universal. Measured with /usr/bin/time -l (instructions retired) on CPython 3.14.0 on an Apple M4 Pro, taking the difference over 30M loop iterations with loop overhead subtracted: x = a + b is about 91 instructions including the add itself; x = o.v is about 70; x = f() is about 230. §4g already removed Fig 7.7's unsourced "~150 instructions" because 3.11+ specialises these paths.
fix: "Every Python statement becomes dozens to hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop, plus the actual work."
reason: Low severity but cheap and safe. "Every ... hundreds" is a universal, unsourced count. The finder's measurement on 3.14 puts x = a + b near 90 instructions, and the specialising interpreter (Fig 7.7 strip) shortens simple paths. "Dozens to hundreds" is defensible for all statements.
judge_fix: ch7-interpret-p3: "Every Python statement becomes dozens to hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop, plus the actual work."

quote: The result was the first interpreter that mattered
problem: This is an overclaim of 'first'. Interpreters were in production use years before Lisp: Mauchly's Short Code on UNIVAC (1950) and Backus's Speedcoding on the IBM 701 (1953), which was widely used and led directly to FORTRAN. The sentence implies those did not matter.
fix: "The result was a working interpreter: a program that read each Lisp expression at runtime and executed it directly, without ever producing a separate binary." The paragraph's first sentence already says it was the first Lisp interpreter.
reason: "First interpreter that mattered" is arguable. Short Code (1949-50) and Speedcoding (IBM 701, 1953) were in real use earlier. The paragraph already says first Lisp interpreter, so the claim can be dropped without loss.
judge_fix: ch7-interpret-p1: "The result was a working interpreter: a program that read each Lisp expression at runtime and executed it directly, without ever producing a separate binary."

quote: ran on an IBM 704 at MIT in 1959 ... who had been transcribing the paper
problem: There are two problems. (1) Date: Russell's two firsthand accounts say McCarthy brought him the half-page eval in October or November 1958, he hand-compiled it for "probably six weeks", and "By December, I had a working interpreter" (Smithsonian NMAH AC1498, 2017). The 2008 CHM oral history says the same: "I got something working before Christmas". McCarthy's accounts put eval in the 1959 paper work, so the primary sources conflict; 1959 is not settled. (2) Neither oral history says Russell was transcribing the paper. Both say he had been hand-compiling Lisp functions into 704 code. Pass 20 declined this flag, citing "I'd been hand-compiling all sorts of things like that", but that quote supports hand-compiling, not transcribing.
fix: "The first Lisp interpreter ran on an IBM 704 at MIT around the turn of 1959." Also replace "who had been transcribing the paper" with "who had spent months hand-translating Lisp functions into machine code". Sources: CHM oral history of Steve Russell, 2008, X4970.2009, pp. 8–9; Smithsonian transcript, 2017.
reason: "Who had been transcribing the paper" is not attested. McCarthy's own history says Russell proposed hand-coding eval, and the ledger's own quote ("hand-compiling all sorts of things like that for two or three months") supports hand-compiling, not transcribing. The 1958 versus 1959 date is a conflict of primary sources (McCarthy's 1976 letter and the CHM catalogue place the work in 1958-59, and I could not open the transcripts), so a hedge is safer than a flat 1959. Low severity.
judge_fix: ch7-interpret-p1: "The first Lisp interpreter ran on an IBM 704 at MIT around the turn of 1959." and "A research assistant named Steve Russell, who had spent months hand-translating Lisp functions into machine code, realised that `eval` looked like working code..."

quote: at 25 ms thread 1 takes the lock back
problem: Fig 7.4 draws T1 running and T2 waiting from 25 ms, but CPython does not hand the GIL back that way. A thread returning from I/O waits for the GIL. Only after one full switch interval (5 ms) with no handoff does it set the drop request (take_gil in Python/ceval_gil.c, the 3.2+ GIL). So T2 keeps running until about 30 ms. The figure's own first three handoffs follow this rule; the fourth breaks it, and it hides the well-known I/O convoy cost.
fix: Desc and drawing: "at 25 ms thread 1's I/O is done and it waits for the lock; thread 2 hands it over when the 5 ms interval runs out, at 30 ms." Draw T1 grey (waits for GIL) and T2 green from 25 to 30 ms.
reason: In CPython 3.2+ a thread returning from I/O waits up to the switch interval (5 ms) before setting the drop request, so T2 keeps the GIL until 30 ms. The figure's first three handoffs follow the 5 ms rule and the fourth breaks it. This is real, though low severity and a small redraw.
judge_fix: Fig 7.4 desc and drawing: "at 25 ms thread 1's I/O is done and it waits for the lock; thread 2 hands it over when the 5 ms interval runs out, at 30 ms." Draw T1 grey (waits for GIL) and T2 green from 25 to 30 ms.

quote: in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs somewhat slower in it.
problem: In 3.13 the overhead was about 40% on pyperformance. That is the same size the prose (ch7-gil-p2) calls a failure ("30–50%"), so "somewhat" understates it and blurs the 3.13 to 3.14 progress the prose describes.
fix: "in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs about 40% slower in it (about 5–10% in 3.14)." Source: docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html ("In 3.13, this overhead is about 40% on the pyperformance suite").
reason: docs.python.org/3.13/howto/free-threading-python.html: "In 3.13, this overhead is about 40% on the pyperformance suite." "Somewhat slower" understates it and blurs the 3.13 to 3.14 progress that ch7-gil-p2 describes. Same finding as 23.
judge_fix: Fig 7.4 strip: "...in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs about 40% slower in it (about 5-10% in 3.14)."

quote: Every Python object carries a count of how many names point to it
problem: The reference count counts every reference: list slots, dict values, attributes and stack entries, not just names. Since ch7-types-p1 defines a variable as a name, a reader can conclude that an object held only in a list has a count of zero and would be freed.
fix: "Every Python object carries a count of how many references point to it (names, list slots, attributes)"
reason: The count covers all references (list slots, attributes, stack), not only names. ch7-types-p1 defines a variable as a name, so "names" is inexact for the one mechanism the paragraph builds on. The fix adds no depth.
judge_fix: ch7-gil-p2: "Every Python object carries a count of how many references point to it (names, list slots, attributes); when the count drops to zero, the object is freed."

quote: Every web framework that accepted pickled session cookies has been bitten by this
problem: This is a universal claim with no source. What is documented is narrower: Django's ticket #29708 says RCEs "continue to happen" despite MAC-signed pickled cookies once a key leaks (PickleSerializer was deprecated in 4.1; JSON has been the default since 1.6), and Pyramid 2.0 switched SignedCookieSessionFactory from pickle to JSON for the same RCE risk. The owner's register here is kept; only the quantifier overreaches.
fix: "Web frameworks that kept sessions in pickled cookies were bitten by this, and moved to JSON;". Keep the rest of the sentence as is. Sources: code.djangoproject.com/ticket/29708; pyramid.readthedocs.io whatsnew-2.0.
reason: "Every web framework" is unsourced and universal. Documented cases are narrower: Django ticket #29708 and the PickleSerializer deprecation, and Pyramid 2.0 moving from pickle to JSON. The owner's register stays.
judge_fix: ch7-datasci-p7: "Several web frameworks that accepted pickled session cookies have been bitten by this;" and keep the rest of the sentence.

quote: it spread into data science, scientific computing and most of the world's introductory programming courses.
problem: There is no global count of introductory courses behind "most". The usual source, Guo 2014 (CACM blog), covers top US CS departments only (8 of the top 10 taught Python first).
fix: "and many of the world's introductory programming courses."
reason: No global count supports "most"; Guo 2014 covers top US departments only. Same finding as 17.
judge_fix: ch7-vanrossum-p1: "...and many of the world's introductory programming courses."

quote: is ten thousand lines of C in a file called `ceval.c`, with a case for every bytecode instruction.
problem: In 3.14, the release the chapter treats as current, ceval.c is 3,731 lines. Since 3.12 the instruction cases are written in bytecodes.c (5,557 lines) and generated into generated_cases.c.h (12,541 lines), which ceval.c includes at line 1127. Ten thousand matches neither the file nor the sum (about 16.3k). Pass 20 declined this flag by counting the include (3.13: about 9.4k), but by that reckoning 3.14 is about 16k. A reader who opens ceval.c finds no switch cases.
fix: Drop the number: "is a loop in C, in a file called `ceval.c`, with a case for every bytecode instruction." Source: python/cpython 3.14 branch, line counts of Python/ceval.c, Python/bytecodes.c and Python/generated_cases.c.h.
reason: Since 3.12 the instruction cases live in bytecodes.c and are generated into generated_cases.c.h, which ceval.c includes. In 3.14 ceval.c itself is a few thousand lines, so "ten thousand" matches neither the file nor the sum (about 16k). A reader who opens ceval.c finds no switch cases in it. The ledger's decline rested on the 3.13 count, which no longer holds for the release the chapter treats as current.
judge_fix: ch7-cpython-p2: "The *evaluator*, the loop from Section 01, lives in a C file called `ceval.c` and has a case for every bytecode instruction."

problem: ch7-interpret-p1 says Russell's Lisp eval was "the first interpreter that mattered". Earlier interpreters were in real use before it: Mauchly's Short Code (UNIVAC, 1949–50) and Backus's Speedcoding (IBM 701, 1953), which led to FORTRAN. The claim is arguable at best; "the first Lisp interpreter" is safe.
reason: Duplicate of 6. Same defect and same fix.
judge_fix: As 6: "The result was a working interpreter: a program that read each Lisp expression at runtime and executed it directly, without ever producing a separate binary."

problem: ch7-interpret-p3 says "Every Python statement becomes hundreds of CPU instructions in that loop". The count has no source and "every" makes it a universal claim. Since 3.11, CPython's specialising interpreter runs a simple statement such as `x = a + b` on small ints in roughly a hundred instructions or fewer, and `pass` compiles to almost nothing. UNDER.md §4g already removed an unsourced "~150 instructions" count from Fig 7.7 for this reason (line 551). "Dozens to hundreds" or "many times the work" would be safer.
reason: Duplicate of 5.
judge_fix: As 5: "dozens to hundreds of CPU instructions".

problem: p1 'He had spent three years on a research language called ABC': van Rossum's own account (python-history.blogspot.com, 'Personal History - part 1, CWI', 2009) gives 'After 4 or 5 years the ABC project was terminated' and calls ABC the language 'on which I'd spent four years of my life'. By late 1989 he had also moved to CWI's Amoeba group. The sentence's 'had spent' allows that, but 'three' contradicts him. Suggested fix: 'four years'. This wording has been in the text since before Pass 27 and has no §4g entry.
reason: Fetched python-history.blogspot.com/2009/01/personal-history-part-1-cwi.html. Van Rossum writes "ABC, on which I'd spent four years of my life" and "After 4 or 5 years the ABC project was terminated". The text says three.
judge_fix: ch7-vanrossum-p1: "He had spent four years on a research language called ABC..."

problem: p1 'most of the world's introductory programming courses': an unsourced overclaim. The usual evidence (Guo 2014) covers only top US computer science departments. 'many' or 'a large share' would hold.
reason: Duplicate of 12.
judge_fix: As 12: "many of the world's introductory programming courses".

problem: Consistency within the section (not a fact error): ABC is 'a research language' in p1 and 'a teaching language' in Fig 7.2, and the spelling is 'USENET' in p1 but 'Usenet' in the figure. Each pair is true, but the reader meets two labels for one thing.
reason: Only the spelling half holds. The text spells it "USENET" in ch7-vanrossum-p1 and in the glossary definition of van Rossum, while Fig 7.2, Part III and Ch18 write "Usenet". "Research language" versus "teaching language" is not a defect: ABC was both, and each label fits its context.
judge_fix: ch7-vanrossum-p1: "In 1991 he posted it to Usenet's discussion groups..." and the same change in the van Rossum glossary definition ("released it to Usenet by 1991"). Leave the ABC labels.

problem: ch7-types-p3: 'a network socket' is given as an object with a read() method, but Python's plain socket.socket has recv()/send() and no read(). Checked locally: hasattr(socket.socket(), 'read') is False. Only ssl.SSLSocket, or the file object returned by sock.makefile(), has read(). The example does not hold for an ordinary Python socket.
reason: Duplicate of 1, verified: a plain socket has no read().
judge_fix: As 1: "(a file, an HTTP response, a stand-in for testing)".

problem: ch7-types-p2: the claim that dynamically typed languages '(Python, JavaScript, Ruby)' run until the mistake 'and dies there with a TypeError' is true of Python and Ruby but not of JavaScript in general. JavaScript usually converts a string passed where a number is wanted instead of raising an error (1 + "a" gives "1a", "5" * 2 gives 10).
reason: Duplicate of 2, verified with node.
judge_fix: As 2: "(Python, Ruby, Lisp)".

problem: Fig 7.4 How it works strip: 'in 3.13 it is optional, and single-threaded code runs somewhat slower in it'. My recollection, not checked against the docs: Python 3.13's free-threading guide gives that build's single-threaded overhead as about 40% on pyperformance, because the specializing interpreter is switched off there. The 'about 5–10%' figure in p2 is the 3.14 result. 'Somewhat' understates the 3.13 cost, and a reader may take 5–10% to be 3.13's number.
reason: Duplicate of 9. The 3.13 docs say about 40%.
judge_fix: As 9: "about 40% slower in it (about 5-10% in 3.14)".

problem: ch7-gil-p2: 'a count of how many names point to it'. CPython counts every reference (list slots, attributes, arguments), not only names. This is likely acceptable at this depth, but strictly it is narrower than the truth.
reason: Duplicate of 10. Wording is slightly narrower than the truth, and the fix costs nothing.
